beats.narration_text: Most validation gives one of two answers, pass or fail. But often the honest answer is neither, because the data to judge isn't there.

props.command: Should a checker only ever say yes or no?
props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · MYCROFT — SEC FILINGS AGENT
output: Sometimes the data to judge isn't there.
A third answer keeps the doubt visible.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Asavari, a fellow at Humanitarians AI. This video is about why a good data checker needs three answers, not two. You'll learn why letting a system say 'I don't know' is more trustworthy than forcing a pass or a fail. If you build or rely on automated checks, this is for you.

props.command: What is this video about, and why should I watch it?
props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · MYCROFT — SEC FILINGS AGENT
output: Who: Asavari, a Humanitarians AI fellow
Why watch: catch the mistake before it costs you

beats.narration_text: To check that a balance sheet balances you need assets, liabilities, and equity. If one is missing, you can't run the check. A two-answer system must pick. Pass is a quiet lie, you didn't verify anything. Fail cries wolf on data that might be fine. Neither tells the truth.

props.artifactTitle: A missing input is not a passing check
artifactLines: forcing PASS is a quiet lie; forcing FAIL cries wolf

beats.narration_text: So every rule returns one of three verdicts. Pass, when the data is present and the check holds. Fail, when it's violated, an impossible margin, a sheet that doesn't balance. And unknown, when the inputs aren't there. Unknown is the system refusing to pretend, surfacing exactly where you can't yet trust the data.

props.artifactTitle: Every check returns one of three verdicts
artifactLines: PASS — data present and the check holds
FAIL — present and the check is violated
UNKNOWN — inputs aren't there to judge (surfaced, not hidden)
props.sparkLine: Let the system say 'I don't know'.

beats.narration_text: Here it is working. A sample reported a gross margin of three hundred and ten percent. Not merely wrong, impossible. A dashboard showed it anyway, because a dashboard doesn't care whether its inputs make sense. A rule three lines long fails it instantly. No model.

artifactLines: A polished dashboard showed it anyway
A three-line rule fails it — no model

beats.narration_text: Ask whether something that validates data for you can say I don't know, or whether it's forced to pretend. Does it catch the truly impossible? When it can't decide, does it tell you? A checker that's always certain is not trustworthy. One that's honest about its limits is. Calibrated doubt beats confident guessing.

props.artifactTitle: Trust a checker that can say 'I don't know'
artifactLines: Can it return 'unknown', or only pass/fail?
Does it flag impossible values, not just odd ones?
When it can't judge, does it say so — loudly?
Confident wrong answer, or honest 'not sure'?
